title: Pricing Collectives by Rounds and Chunks
summary: Apply the critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ to classify communication workloads into latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.

sections: Pricing Collectives by Rounds and Chunks

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Pricing Collectives by Rounds and Chunks** in *Collective Communication* (Vol II). By the end you should be able to:

- Apply the critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ to classify communication workloads into latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes
- Explain the NCCL reality gap by contrasting software stack launch overheads in small messages with wire saturation in large payloads

blocks.source: Vol II, Collective Communication, § Pricing Collectives by Rounds and Chunks
blocks.md: A gradient bucket, the group of gradient tensors reduced in one call, can reach tens of megabytes, large enough to saturate a single network link. Yet when a thousand-GPU ring divides that bucket into a thousand shards, each hop moves only tens of kilobytes and can spend more time starting the transfer than sending its bytes. Pricing a collective therefore requires separating the fixed time to initiate each message from the rate at which bytes move once in transit.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md: Pay attention to: The alpha-beta price charged once per schedule round on a chunk; The critical message size n* = alpha * beta separating latency-bound from bandwidth-bound steps; Why small-message collectives diverge most from bare-wire predictions; The ordered hierarchy of cost models through calibration.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain why small-message collective timings can exceed a bare-wire prediction by a much larger relative factor than large-message timings. Which measurements are needed before using this difference in a cluster capacity plan?
blocks.md: Small transfers can spend most of their time in launch, descriptor preparation, registration, proxy processing, and synchronization rather than serialization. For large transfers, the payload-over-bandwidth term can dominate those fixed costs. Benchmark effective startup latency and sustained bandwidth for the intended message sizes, placement, and concurrent traffic. The discrepancy is configuration-dependent, so an illustrative overhead ratio is not a measured hardware guarantee.

questions.q: A single-transfer model uses effective startup cost $\alpha=1.5\,\mu\text{s}$ and per-direction bandwidth $\beta=50\text{ GB/s}$. Which conclusion follows for a 4 KB transfer, and what must be added before classifying a complete gradient AllReduce?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The single-transfer terms are equal at alphabeta=75 KB. A 4 KB transfer therefore spends more modeled time in startup than in byte transfer. Fusion of compatible ready messages or a lower-overhead path are candidates, with packing and readiness costs included. For a ring AllReduce of an M-byte tensor over N ranks, compare each M/N chunk with the knee and count \$2(N-1) rounds; the full tensor’s size alone does not classify the schedule. Compression only removes byte-transfer work and must also win against encoding, aggregation, and quality costs.
questions.hint: Think about: apply the critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ to classify communication workloads into latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.
options: The single-transfer knee is 75 KB, so startup dominates the 4 KB transfer. A complete AllReduce additionally requires the schedule’s round count and chunk size, then calibration for its placement.
The 4 KB transfer is bandwidth-bound because adding ranks makes every individual transfer saturate its port.
The 75 KB knee is a maximum buffer size, so larger messages cannot be sent over this link.
The critical message size defines the maximum possible buffer size that can be transferred in a single CUDA stream without host CPU intervention.

points: You can now apply the critical message size $n^* = \alpha \cdot \beta$ to classify communication workloads into latency-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.
You can now explain the NCCL reality gap by contrasting software stack launch overheads in small messages with wire saturation in large payloads.
